title: Is the In-House Counsel Movement Going Global? A Preliminary Assessment of the Role of Internal Counsel in Emerging Economies
pub: Wisconsin Law Review, Vol. 2012, No. 2, pp. 251–304 (2012)
author: David B. Wilkins

dup.label: is in house counsel movement going global preliminary assessment role internal counsel in emerging economies

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Corporate buyers: Insourcing and partnerships coexist
st.an: Wilkins accepts that in-house counsel are gaining control over legal purchasing without simply displacing law firms, and materially develops the proposition by showing that department size is not a proxy for authority or savings and that globalization produces jurisdiction-specific forms of buyer power and professional status.
qs: At the same time, this preliminary evidence also suggests that the processes by which this largely U.S.-inspired model is diffusing in the BIC countries is likely to produce important differences in the way that internal counsel conceive of and operationalize their roles both within and among these important jurisdictions.

st.t: General counsel: Strategic authority carries guardian tension
st.an: Wilkins accepts the rise of general counsel as a centre of corporate authority and develops the cluster’s proposition through a six-dimensional framework that separates department size from authority, purchasing control and professional standing. He materially extends it by showing that global diffusion is context-dependent, with managerial influence and professional independence remaining distinct and uneven achievements.
qs: The Relationship with the Boss Although the most visible manifestation of the in-house counsel movement in the United States is the increasing control that GCs exercise over outside counsel, in many respects the most important outcome of the movement has been the growing power and visibility of internal lawyers within the hierarchies of corporate decision making.

At the same time, this preliminary evidence also suggests that the processes by which this largely U.S.-inspired model is diffusing in the BIC countries is likely to produce important differences in the way that internal counsel conceive of and operationalize their roles both within and among these important jurisdictions.

st.t: Global legal markets: Liberalization remains locally contested
st.an: The source accepts that globalization diffuses U.S.-inspired in-house practices without producing uniform convergence, and materially develops the cluster through a six-dimensional, jurisdiction-sensitive framework separating staffing and credentials from purchasing power, internal authority, professional standing and policy influence.
qs: At the same time, this preliminary evidence also suggests that the processes by which this largely U.S.-inspired model is diffusing in the BIC countries is likely to produce important differences in the way that internal counsel conceive of and operationalize their roles both within and among these important jurisdictions.

st.t: Buyer authority: In-house growth need not displace firms
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal distinction: GCs gained authority by diagnosing legal needs and controlling purchasing decisions, while expanded in-house capacity did not reliably reduce reliance on firms or outside spending. It also reinforces the cluster’s cautions that strategic standing and international diffusion are uneven and cannot be inferred from department size or recruitment alone.
qs: Notwithstanding a significant investment in building up in-house capacities, many companies discovered that outside spending on law firms continued to escalate throughout the 1990s and into the first decade of the twenty166.

st.t: General counsel: Corporate leadership may weaken independence
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis: globalization encourages stronger, more strategically integrated in-house legal functions, but neither convergence on the US model nor professional independence is assured. It specifically warns that integration into corporate teams, weak independence norms and local institutional conditions may undermine counsel’s gatekeeping role.

st.t: In-house power: Business integration risks professional capture
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s core account: in-house counsel gained substantial purchasing and organizational power, but their integration into business teams can compromise independent gatekeeping. He also reinforces the cluster’s qualifications that outside-firm displacement is limited and that professional authority varies across jurisdictions.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source broadly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that technology is more likely to redesign and redistribute legal work than eliminate lawyers wholesale. It considers technology-driven decentralisation and substitution plausible, but rejects automatic professional demise and emphasizes continuing demand for independent, context-rich, integrated legal and business judgment. It does not materially address jagged AI capability, verification or deployment governance.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source supports the buyer-power and insourcing elements of the cluster by describing the increased influence of in-house counsel and citing direct hiring of law graduates as a cost-saving substitute for BigLaw associates. It does not address AI-enabled workflow segmentation, outcome pricing, verification, or the broader durability of the billable-hour model.
qs: 11, 2011), http://www.abajournal.com/news/article/ some_corps_cut_costs_by_hiring_attorneys (describing Pfizer’s program and quoting the general counsel of HP as saying that such hiring was likely to be “the wave of the future”).

Indeed, in a move that would have been unthinkable just a few years ago, outside law firms have begun to recruit partners laterally from inhouse legal departments in order to acquire their experience and connections, strengthen relationships with existing clients, and to recruit new ones.10 All of this has profoundly restructured traditional mobility patterns and prestige hierarchies within the U.S.

kp.k: Global diffusion is a preliminary finding, not established convergence
kp.d: Wilkins reports preliminary GLEE research, including conversations with over one-hundred general counsels of local and foreign companies in Brazil, India, and China, suggesting that the in-house counsel movement is spreading. He anticipates differences within and among jurisdictions rather than automatic replication of the U.S. model. This historical analysis concerns globalization and professional organization, not measured effects of AI.
qs: On the basis of preliminary research, including conversations with over one-hundred general counsels of both “local” and “foreign” companies in the BIC countries, we have determined that there are already important indications that the in-house counsel movement is indeed “going global” to these emerging economies.
What follows, therefore, should be viewed as an attempt to stimulate conversation rather than an effort to resolve the question posed by the title to this Article.

kp.k: In-house authority rests on three interconnected claims
kp.d: Wilkins identifies economic, substantive, and professional arguments underlying the U.S. movement: internal lawyers could control outside spending, offer better advice through business knowledge, and exercise independent professional judgment despite employee status. These are the movement's legitimating claims, not proof that internal advice is invariably cheaper, better, or more independent.
qs: The first was strictly economic.

Not only are inside lawyers cheaper than their external counterparts, proponents of the inside counsel movement began to declare, but the advice they give corporate managers is likely to be better as well.
Finally, this substantive claim furthered a third professional argument for increasing the standing and prestige of internal counsel.

kp.k: Internal counsel became legal diagnosticians and purchasing agents
kp.d: The U.S. transformation shifted work from outside firms to corporate legal departments and gave general counsel greater responsibility for selecting and managing providers. It also changed career mobility and prestige: in-house departments recruited experienced law-firm lawyers, while firms increasingly recruited partners from corporate departments. Wilkins qualifies absolute growth by noting that in-house employment grew more slowly than the bar overall.
qs: These lawyers now regularly perform legal work traditionally done by outside counsel.

Specifically, today’s general counsel (GC) routinely act as both “diagnosticians” of their company’s legal needs, and as the primary “purchasing agents” deciding whether those needs will be served by an inside lawyer or by an outside firm—and if the work is sent outside, which firm will receive the business.
the overall rate of growth in the number of internal counsel has been slower than the expansion of the bar as a whole.

kp.k: Russian evidence challenges automatic modernization through market liberalization
kp.d: Wilkins uses Kathryn Hendley's 1997 survey of 328 Russian enterprises and 1998 case studies of six companies to caution against assuming that privatization produces powerful internal counsel. Lawyers remained marginal, with weaker credentials, low political and demographic status, and managers skeptical of legal solutions. Limited contact with Western investors and firms constrained exposure to alternative roles. Wilkins stresses the findings' historical and jurisdictional limits.
qs: In 1997, Hendley and her team of researchers conducted a survey of 328 Russian enterprises to see how these companies were using internal legal expertise in the eight years since the fall of communism.
In 1998, Hendley followed up her survey with in-depth case studies of six of the companies in her sample, including direct observation of the work being done by the internal lawyers at each firm.
In the final analysis, Hendley concludes that the role of internal counsel was little changed from what it had been in the former Soviet Union under Communism.
As Hendley herself is careful to note, her conclusions may only apply to Russia—and indeed Russia at a particular time in that country’s history.

kp.k: Globalization transmits demand, knowledge, and regulatory complexity
kp.d: Wilkins proposes three mechanisms for diffusion: economic globalization creates cross-border demand; knowledge globalization transmits professional models through education, employment, associations, and publications; governance globalization increases interacting national and transnational obligations. Outbound investment by emerging-market companies further increases demand for sophisticated advice. These mechanisms are proposed explanations and expectations, not demonstrated causal effects.
qs: As foreign companies locate more of their resources in the BIC countries, it is likely that these sophisticated players will increasingly want inhouse lawyers who will support these operations in the same way that the companies’ existing operations are supported in more established markets.
A key source of transmission is the formal education system itself, especially when combined with the movement of people.
international and transnational regulation increasingly plays a key role in governing the affairs of companies that compete in the global economy.

Needless to say, there is certainly no guarantee that economic globalization, the globalization of knowledge, and the globalization of governance will necessarily produce sophisticated in-house counsel

kp.k: Department size is an unreliable proxy for authority
kp.d: Wilkins reports that his study of S&P 500 legal departments found a median of thirty-five lawyers but a range from near-total outsourcing to over 1000 lawyers. The five largest departments spent a higher-than-average share of their legal budgets externally. Sako and Susskind likewise found that small departments could exercise substantial outside-counsel control. Large state-owned-enterprise departments could instead consist of low-status bureaucrats.
qs: Nevertheless, even in the United States size remains an imperfect measure of prestige and power.

we found that the median legal department employed thirtyfive lawyers, but that the range in size was quite significant, with some companies having almost completely outsourced their legal function and others maintaining legal departments of over 1000 lawyers.
Indeed, the five largest legal departments in our sample spent a higher percentage of their legal budget on outside law firms than average.
Some small legal departments, who outsource most of the company’s legal work, exercise a high degree of control over outside law firms while others do not.

kp.k: Brazilian survey separates staffing scale from claimed responsibility
kp.d: A cited Brazilian study found that 63% of departments had one to five lawyers and only 8% had more than thirty. Nonetheless, 75% of surveyed general counsels claimed outside-counsel hiring authority, and 96% claimed at least shared responsibility for complex and recurrent matters, including 30% claiming primary responsibility. Wilkins contrasts these self-reports with concerns about careers, resources, and management participation, rather than treating claimed authority as verified practice.
qs: A recent report of Brazilian in-house departments, for example, found that the overwhelming majority (63%) had between one and five lawyers, and only 8% had more than thirty lawyers.
Although such statements echo the claims of the in-house counsel movement, there are also indications that the reality on the ground may not yet live up to these bold pronouncements.

kp.k: Credentials improve, but career attractiveness remains uncertain
kp.d: Preliminary interviews suggest rising credentials among internal lawyers in state-owned and private companies, including international qualifications and law-firm experience. In 2010, more than twenty percent of graduates from India's three top National Law Schools accepted corporate legal department jobs. Wilkins cautions that this may reflect limited alternatives rather than preference over law firms; entry-level corporate salaries remained lower, and senior compensation parity was unestablished.
qs: For example in 2010, more than twenty percent of all of the graduates from India’s three top National Law Schools accepted jobs in corporate legal departments.

Whether this increase in status in the lawyers joining in-house legal departments constitutes the kind of elevation in the role of internal legal counsel trumpeted by the in-house counsel movement, however, remains to be seen.
Entry-level salaries in corporate law offices remain significantly lower than they are in top law firms

kp.k: Gender and professional status interact rather than move uniformly
kp.d: Wilkins contrasts Russia, where women's overrepresentation reinforced low in-house status, with the United States, where growing female participation coincided with the movement's increasing authority. He argues that female general counsels could use purchasing influence to promote gender equity, while emphasizing that men still held most top positions. Preliminary Brazilian observations identify a female-GC network pursuing hiring and promotion changes.
qs: Because female lawyers entered into corporate legal departments at the beginning of the in-house counsel movement, these positions have actually risen in power and prestige as they have become more feminized.

Indeed, female general counsels have used their growing influence over legal purchasing decisions to press for gender equity (and to a lesser extent other forms of diversity) in the profession as a whole.
Nevertheless, it is important to recognize that men continue to occupy the overwhelming majority of top positions inside corporate legal departments.

kp.k: Purchasing power changes pricing without eliminating enduring firm relationships
kp.d: Wilkins reports that only about 20% of surveyed S&P 500 general counsels frequently terminated important firm relationships within the preceding three years; over 30% never did, and almost 50% did so once or twice. Nevertheless, preliminary emerging-market evidence indicates competitive selection, preferred-provider panels, discounts, alternative fees, and direct oversight. A cited Brazilian survey reported 46% requiring fixed or previously agreed prices, 19% using success fees, and 3% using unlimited hourly pricing.
qs: Only about 20% of GCs from S&P 500 companies reported terminating such relationships “frequently” within the last three years, while over 30% had never done so, with another almost 50% having done so only once or twice.

The relevant question, therefore, is whether GCs in emerging jurisdictions are also using their power over corporate purchasing decisions to restructure the relationship between companies and their outside law firms and to drive changes in the internal structure and operation of firms.

kp.k: Internalization reflects business knowledge and professional status struggles
kp.d: Wilkins reports that emerging-market internal counsel justify taking work inside through superior knowledge of company needs, alongside cost pressures. Preliminary Indian interviews also reveal resentment of outside lawyers' perceived arrogance, potentially intensified by concentrated corporate expertise and social hierarchy. He presents this status reversal as a possible catalyst, not an established causal finding.
qs: While our interviews with in-house counsel in the United States also uncovered evidence that these lawyers sometimes feel “offended” by what they perceive as arrogance by outside lawyers, the level of resentment seems far higher in India.

Although we are still at the preliminary stage of understanding this phenomenon, the fact that a few corporate lawyers in India have had a virtual monopoly on sophisticated corporate work and the hierarchical nature of business relationships in India—a hierarchy reinforced by caste, religion, region, and social class—appear to play a significant role.

kp.k: Executive influence depends on business, legal, and political relationships
kp.d: In developed markets, Wilkins describes general counsels gaining strategic responsibilities and oversight of adjacent functions. Emerging-market influence is less uniform: family-company counsel may derive authority from personal ties, while state involvement may privilege political access over legal competence. He predicts that overseas listings and acquisitions will increase demand for legal expertise by exposing companies to less negotiable foreign regulatory regimes.
qs: Many also oversee other related corporate functions, such as public relations, government affairs, human resources, and compliance.
These internal lawyers tend to work for family-owned companies or groups and have a very strong relationship, often cemented by social or familial bonds, with the controlling shareholder.
his biggest challenge is to convince his managers, all of whom are senior government officials, that legal restrictions have to be taken as seriously as political ones in operating the company.

kp.k: Professional independence remains contested despite increased commercial authority
kp.d: Wilkins treats professional status as an organized project, supported by associations such as ACC, rather than an automatic consequence of functionality. He reports critics' concerns that employed lawyers cannot independently police corporate misconduct, proposals for reporting to independent board committees, and European resistance to privilege claims. In emerging economies, inferior or separate credentials and fragmented constituencies may hinder collective status-building.
qs: some academic commentators have begun to challenge whether internal counsel are too dependent on their corporate employers to act as independent gatekeepers

some have gone so far as to argue that to become truly independent, general counsels should be removed from the control of corporate managers and report only to an independent committee of the company’s board.
At the core of this decision is a fundamental doubt about whether “employed” lawyers can ever truly be “independent.”

kp.k: Corporate counsel can shape public outcomes through private rules
kp.d: Wilkins argues that general counsels influence public policy through lobbying and through company policies where legal standards are incomplete or contradictory, such as supplier child-labor rules. Such private ordering may have substantial practical effects. He remains uncertain whether emerging-market counsel regard this as central to their mission or can replicate U.S. influence, given different political and legal contexts.
qs: general counsels—particularly those in large multinational companies— are often in the position of deciding key public policy issues themselves.
It is not clear, however, that general counsels in emerging countries view either lobbying or socially conscious private ordering as a core part of their mission—at least not formally.

It is quite possible, for example, that the influence of ACC and other similar organizations in the United States is as much a function of America’s highly legalistic culture as it is of the power of in-house lawyers.

kp.k: Business-team integration may weaken independent gatekeeping
kp.d: Wilkins reports Rosen's 2002 reassessment of legal departments previously studied in the 1980s: integration into functional project teams could make legal value more visible while changing lawyers' identification and risk judgments. Rosen warns that counsel might become consultants who prioritize business objectives and the appearance of independence. Wilkins treats this as an important critique, not proof that all integrated counsel lose independence.
qs: lawyers who come to identify too closely with business teams may begin to “approach managing legal risks with non-compliance as a viable option.”

Rather than being the independent counselors trumpeted by the in-house counsel movement, Rosen concludes, internal lawyers in the twentyfirst century are in danger of becoming just another “consultant” with no more independence or distinctiveness than any other corporate employee.

kp.k: Standardized technology could displace customized advice and centralized departments
kp.d: Wilkins reports Larry Ribstein's prediction that smart technology and process-based solutions could erode in-house lawyers' power and replace departments with legally trained staff dispersed across businesses. Wilkins considers it possible that emerging-market companies might adopt this approach especially readily. These are prospective arguments about standardized technology in 2012, not findings about generative AI, agents, or realized job displacement.
qs: Professor Larry Ribstein argues “in-house lawyers ultimately may find their own power eroded by products and services that replace customized legal advice with standardized technology.”
As a result, Ribstein claims, “in-house legal departments” may be replaced “by law-trained people dispersed throughout the organization.”

it is certainly possible that corporations in these jurisdictions may be even more willing to look for “smart” solutions that allow them to turn to relatively inexpensive “law-trained” employees rather than to develop the kind of powerful and independent in-house lawyers contemplated by the inhouse counsel movement.

kp.k: Complexity and independence may counter technological substitution
kp.d: Wilkins rejects treating the decline of independent lawyers as inevitable. He argues that clients and lawyers both benefit from credible professional independence, while growing global legal, political, and social complexity may sustain demand for integrated business and legal advice. The unresolved research question is how counsel balance business partnership and senior-management membership with professional independence.
qs: Nevertheless, one should also not automatically assume that these larger forces will prevent general counsel in the BIC countries from emerging as influential and independent advisors.

Although the pressures Rosen and Ribstein identify are certainly real and important, both lawyers and clients have reason to push against them in order to realize the benefits that they can both only receive if the legal profession credibly maintains its status as an “independent” profession.

the growing complexity of the global legal, political, and social environment in which companies increasingly operate is likely to put a premium on gaining access to the kind of integrated business and legal advice that sophisticated in-house lawyers claim to offer.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Wilkins conditionally predicts that smart legal technology could enable emerging-market companies to use less expensive law-trained employees instead of building powerful, independent in-house legal departments. The article discusses smart technology, not AI explicitly.
pts.d: In the conclusion (pp. 303–304), Wilkins considers, without fully endorsing, a technology-driven alternative to the spread of the U.S. in-house counsel model. He suggests that companies in emerging economies, particularly India and China, may be especially receptive to technological solutions that substitute law-trained employees for independent in-house lawyers. Combined with integration into business teams and weaker traditions of professional independence, this could alter internal counsel's gatekeeping role. The stronger claims that standardized technology will erode in-house lawyers' power and replace legal departments originate in Larry Ribstein's work, which Wilkins discusses as a critique rather than presents as his own established finding. Wilkins also offers a countervailing prediction: increasing global complexity could increase demand for sophisticated, integrated legal and business advice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The technology-related predictions rest on cited scholarly arguments and contextual reasoning, not AI performance measurements or direct empirical tests of technology-driven substitution.
pts.d: Wilkins draws on Ribstein's argument about standardized technology replacing customized advice and Rosen's account of legal departments being reorganized into business project teams. His extension to emerging markets rests on the role of new technologies in those economies' development and the comparatively weaker professional-independence norms in some jurisdictions. The wider article draws on preliminary GLEE research, including conversations with more than one hundred general counsel, but does not present these conversations as direct evidence that smart technology has displaced in-house lawyers. No AI benchmarks, measured productivity gains, or technology-attributable employment effects are reported.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: These are open-ended, conditional prospects advanced in 2012, with no deadline or quantified adoption trajectory.
pts.d: Technology-driven substitution is framed as a possibility, especially where companies readily adopt new technologies and professional independence is less established. The risk to independent legal gatekeeping is also conditional on lawyers' integration into self-managing business teams. Wilkins expressly rejects treating these forces as inevitably preventing the emergence of influential, independent general counsel. He leaves their ultimate effects as questions for further research.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal departments, general counsel, law-trained employees, and their corporate employers, particularly in emerging economies.
pts.d: The potential organizational change concerns the buyer side of the corporate legal market: companies could rely on lower-cost law-trained staff rather than develop autonomous legal departments. In-house lawyers could lose authority or become more closely identified with business teams, potentially weakening their independent compliance role. Corporate managers could gain access to standardized legal solutions, while legal compliance and the profession's public purposes could be affected by changes in gatekeeping. Conversely, companies operating in complex global environments may continue to need sophisticated in-house lawyers capable of integrating legal and business advice. These are not claims about consumer access to justice or measured law-firm job losses.
